title: What Is the Septuagint, and Why Does It Matter?
subtitle: The first churches read their Scriptures in Greek translation, and the New Testament quotes it on nearly every page. Knowing that should steady you, not shake you.

sections.title: How Israel's Scriptures Learned Greek
sections.body:
By the third century BC, large numbers of Jews lived outside the land, and many of them spoke Greek, not Hebrew. Their children were losing the language of Moses. So in Alexandria, the great Greek city of Egypt, Jewish scholars translated the Torah into Greek, and over the following century and beyond, the prophets and the writings followed.

A later legend, told in the Letter of Aristeas, credited the work to seventy-two translators, which is why the translation is called the Septuagint, from the Latin for seventy, abbreviated LXX. The legend grew in the telling. The translation itself was real, and it became the Bible of the Greek-speaking Jewish world, read every Sabbath in the synagogues of Alexandria, Antioch, Asia Minor, and Rome.

That made it the Bible of the early church, too. When the apostles carried the gospel out of Judea, they didn't first have to translate the Scriptures for the nations, because God had seen to that two centuries before Bethlehem. The Word was already waiting in the language of the streets.

sections.title: Why the Quotation Does Not Match Your Old Testament
sections.body:
Every careful reader notices it sooner or later. You follow a New Testament quotation back to your Old Testament and the words don't quite match. Hebrews 10 quotes Psalm 40 as saying a body you have prepared for me, but your Psalm 40 says my ears you have opened. Matthew hears Isaiah 7 promising that the virgin shall conceive, where your Isaiah may read young woman.

Most of the time the New Testament writers were quoting the Septuagint, the version their readers knew, the way a preacher today quotes the translation in the pews, and nobody calls that sloppy. Sometimes the Greek translators rendered a Hebrew idiom interpretively. At other times, as the Dead Sea Scrolls have shown, they were translating a Hebrew text that differed slightly from the one later standardized. The Scrolls contain Hebrew manuscripts that agree with the Septuagint against the medieval Hebrew text in a number of places.

So the differences you notice aren't cracks in the foundation. They're the visible grain of a long, careful, human process, and God didn't go around that process. He worked through it, as he always has.

sections.title: What the Scriptures Meant in the First Century
sections.body:
When Jesus says the Scriptures testify about him, which shelf is he pointing to? The risen Lord names it himself in Luke 24, the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms, the threefold shape Jewish tradition still uses. That core, Torah, the prophets, the psalms, was firm and universally received. The outer edges were still being discussed, and a few books were debated for generations.

Greek-speaking communities also read and treasured books composed or preserved in Greek, the books later called deuterocanonical, like Maccabees and Wisdom of Solomon. That history, not some modern conspiracy, is why Catholic and Protestant Old Testaments differ in length today.

Remember, too, what a Bible physically was. It was a cabinet of scrolls kept at the synagogue, expensive and shared, nothing like the bound volume on your nightstand. People heard Scripture far more than they read it, and they memorized it to a degree that shames us, so when Jesus says it is written, he's appealing to words his hearers carry inside them. The first century didn't own its Bibles, but it knew them.

sections.title: Oral Torah and the Living Conversation
sections.body:
In the first century, Scripture came wrapped in interpretation; it never traveled alone. The Pharisees cultivated what they called the tradition of the elders, an oral Torah applying the written commands to daily life, the tradition Jesus engages in Mark 7. In the synagogues of the land, the Hebrew reading was followed by an Aramaic paraphrase, the targum, which often explained as it translated. Teachers debated texts by linking verse to verse, the method later collected in the midrash.

The New Testament was written inside that conversation, and it argues like a participant. Jesus proves the resurrection from the tense of a verb in Exodus 3, exactly the kind of close reading his contemporaries practiced. Paul, trained under Gamaliel, chains quotations the way the schools did. The early church inherited the habit of reading Scripture about the Messiah from a culture that already read Scripture toward the future, and what it added was the news that the future had arrived.

None of this flattens the Bible into its background. It means the Bible spoke a living language to living readers, and it still expects to.

sections.title: Confidence, Not Anxiety
sections.body:
Some believers hear all this, the translations and variant texts and debated edges and oral traditions, and feel the floor tilt. If that's the history, what exactly am I holding? Take a breath, and then look at what the history actually shows.

It shows a God who was content to give his word in translation from the beginning, whose apostles called a Greek version Scripture without embarrassment. It shows transmission careful enough that the Isaiah scroll found at Qumran, a thousand years older than our previous Hebrew copies, reads recognizably as the Isaiah in your lap. And the variety we can now see is the same variety the first Christians read, preached, and died trusting. Nothing has been discovered that they were protected from, because the faith was born with its eyes open.

It also takes away one of our favorite excuses. The apostles had no leather-bound certainty, no single perfect edition, and they turned the world over with what they had. We have more access to the text than any generation in history and often less appetite for it. The Scriptures have always been able to bear our weight. What's left open is whether we'll finally put it down on them.
